To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the host response to a progressively growing tumour is a biphasic process, consisting of an initial period of increased responsiveness to tumour antigens and a subsequent period of decreased responsiveness.
the stimulation of DNA synthesis by tumour antigens is suppressed in the host bearing the tumour.

the stimulation of DNA synthesis of lymph node cells of tumour bearing mice, as measured by in vitro incorporation of 3H-Td R, is suppressed in the presence of a progressively growing tumour and that this suppression is related to the tumours mass.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the immunological mechanisms involved in tumour-host interactions.
studies on the stimulation and inhibition of DNA synthesis in tumour-bearing hosts and on the role of the tumour in the production of "suppressor factor" in the host.
the elucidation of mechanisms of host resistance to progressively growing tumours and the possible role of suppressor cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a tumour can grow progressively in the host because it is not rejected by the host, not because the host is incapable of rejecting it.

the host's ability to reject the tumur is dependent upon a balance between the stimulatory effect of the tumour antigen on the host's immunocompetent cell and the suppressive effect of the tumur on the same cells.
the host response to a tumour is not simply the result of a single mechanism but rather a composite of several factors which may be operating in a sequential fashion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the host responsiveness is dependent on the balance between the stimulator and suppressor factors, and that the suppressor factors are more effective in the tumour bearing hosts.

the host responsiveness to a progressively-growing methylcholanthene (MCA) induced tumour, MC6/2, was studied at varying time intervals following the implantation of the tumour by monitoring the in vivo incorporation of 3H-Td.R into LNC undergoing stimulation in vivo.
the tumour host becomes "hyporesponsive" due to a "suppressor mechanism" which is initiated by the tumour and which is dependent on the size of the tumour mass.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the failure to reject the tumours in the present situation is due to the development of a hyporeactive state in the host, which may be dependent on the development of an immunological "suppressor factor" that may be responsible for the inhibition of the DNA synthesis in lymphoid cells in vivo.
the host responsiveness to a progressivelygrowing tumour is not a constant function but is dependent on the size and growth rate of the tumour.

the failure to reject the tumur in the situation described is dependent in considerable part on the development of hyporeactivity due to the partial inactivation of the DNA synthetic activity in lymphoid cells, possibly T cells, due to the action of suppressor factor(s) interacting with the lymphoid cells.
